item.title: Iran-based campaign used ChatGPT to plant articles in news outlets, OpenAI says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
“The bill will follow Americans beyond the fighting itself,” an opinion piece in the Port St. Joe Star, a tiny Florida weekly newspaper, warned of the Iran war last month. The article ran under the byline Ervin Hoskins, which has also appeared on articles critical of the war in larger publications including Daily Kos and Middle East Monitor, which together have more than 3 million followers on Facebook. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But ChatGPT maker OpenAI said Thursday that Hoskins’s purported work was generated using its chatbot by users based in Iran as part of an “influence campaign.” The campaign placed about 100 fake articles across at least 20 news outlets, the company said. The author photo on the Hoskins column published by the Star was generated using OpenAI’s artificial intelligence tools, according to the company’s online verification tool. As artificial intelligence tools have become more powerful, some news outlets have been forced to delete AI-generated content published under fake bylines that initially went undetected by editors. Business Insider and Wired removed a series of articles last year that appeared under the byline Margaux Blanchard and appeared to be AI-generated. But while it was unclear who or what was behind the stories written by Blanchard and some other apparently fake personas, OpenAI said in a Thursday report on use of ChatGPT in political influence campaigns that Hoskins was part of an operation focused on spreading content about U.S. military action in Iran. Many of the articles highlighted negative impacts of the war on Americans. OpenAI said that Hoskins was among seven bylines that appeared on the series of AI-generated articles, made by users who sent instructions to the chatbot in Persian. The operations appeared to be run by a commercial outfit as a “for-hire influence campaign,” the company said. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI). David Adlerstein, publisher of the Port St. Joe Star, said in an email that the Hoskins column had caught his eye after it was pitched to him by a PeaceVoice, a small liberal think tank in Oregon, that had been sending the Star content for “years.” Gulf County, where Port St. Joe is located, has a population of about 15,000. “Because we’re in a very red part of Florida, I usually don’t run PeaceVoice columns, but this one struck me as thought-provoking and not a strident attack on Mr. Trump, which would be problematic for much of our readership,” Adlerstein said. Due to his existing relationship with PeaceVoice, he did not feel a need to verify the origin or the column or the author’s identity, he said. Tom Hastings, the founding director of PeaceVoice, said the organization beefed up its existing no-AI policy after OpenAI contacted him. OpenAI said it had banned the accounts behind the campaign and that it blocks access to ChatGPT from Iran. “The overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, but we are unable to identify the particular actor involved,” the company said in its report. “We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.” Middle East Monitor and Daily Kos said they had taken down the articles written by the fake bylines and were reviewing their processes to prevent further incidents. The Daily Kos articles by Hoskins appeared on a community platform not subject to review by the outlet’s staff before publication. Markos Moulitsas, the site’s founder, said in an email that such a campaign was “incredibly corrosive” to the platform. “We already struggle with community members accusing others of being bots or fake accounts simply because they disagree with them. An operation like this pours gasoline on that fire,” he said. “The very trust of our community is at stake.” Articles written by authors OpenAI said were part of the Iranian campaign covered a range of topics in the Middle East but were often critical of the Iran war’s effects on Americans. Many of the outlets were focused on policy and foreign affairs. After generating articles in English, the ChatGPT users in Iran prompted the chatbot to adjust the draft to fit submission criteria for a specific outlet and to generate a pitch email to send to an editor there. The purported authors of the articles were described as freelance writers, policy analysts and peace advocates. The Middle East Monitor, which brands itself as supportive of the Palestinian cause, had published at least 21 stories under bylines OpenAI said were fake including Hoskins, Michael Harrison, Jenny Williams and Alice Johnson. Some of the bylines, including Hoskins, also appear on social media accounts, and in one case a profile on blogging platform Medium, that shared a name and profile image with published articles. An email account apparently used to send the Hoskins article to PeaceVoice, and a LinkedIn account in his name with a photo that appeared with some bylines, did not respond to a request for comment. At least one other purported author, Ericka Feusier, used an AI-generated profile picture, according to OpenAI’s tool that verifies whether images were generated using the company’s technology. OpenAI’s report on influence campaigns mounted using its technology also described a cluster of ChatGPT accounts in Russia that were banned after they were used to operate what appeared to be a fake think tank in Latin America. OpenAI said there was evidence the project may have co-opted real humans to work for the organization. The AI company said that it published the research to inform regulators, other companies and the public of “how we see threat actors trying to leverage AI, and to shine a light on the vulnerabilities they try to exploit.” The outlets impacted by the campaign vary in reach. But while they appear to have published AI-generated articles under fake bylines, real people have read them. Hoskins’s column in the Star prompted a letter to the editor - a rare event for an opinion piece about a national topic, Adlerstein said. He added that he is now looking into introducing an explicit AI policy. Hastings, of PeaceVoice, said the article appeared to be genuine when he saw it. “I found nothing remarkably pro-Iran in his work, which I would never publish, just a legitimate critique of Trump’s war of choice. If Mr Hoskins sends in another I will simply require that we meet by Zoom to discuss,” he wrote in an email. “At least for now, that’s the best I can do.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/09/chatgpt-users-iran-planted-ai-generated-articles-us-news-media/

item.title: Anthropic AI sent a fake murder tip to Philadelphia police while running a test
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Police said Anthropic's AI model was running a test when it filed false information about an unsolved murder in Philadelphia (ANDREJ IVANOV) An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, authorities said Friday, criticizing the company for taking two months to report the incident. The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings. According to Anthropic's account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder. The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case. The incident echoed other recent cases of unintended behavior involving AI models, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face. The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry's increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision. Anthropic published a report Friday outlining multiple types of "unintended" actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website. Other organizations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies, the report said. The newly revealed incidents "had minimal real-world impact" and were "significantly less severe" than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said. The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting "basic" coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits. Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now "until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures... reliably catch behaviors like these," the report said. Philadelphia police said the phony tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department's Real-Time Crime Center for vetting. They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised. Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said. The company alerted the department on October 7, and the two sides met the following day. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable," the department said. Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide." "Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers," the statement added. arp/smb/acb This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/anthropic-ai-model-sent-fake-221343703.html

item.title: Zelensky says Trump gave Putin a 'happy birthday present' with diesel deal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Trump in Washington on Wednesday. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine. Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”. In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran. “I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote. “Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.” He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.” Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach. Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery. The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions. “This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.” Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement. “Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X . “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.” Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week. In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”. “It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said. Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war. Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”. “That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said. Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve. The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.” But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal. Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition. This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/zelenskyy-furious-trump-announces-deal-233931848.html

item.title: U.S. targets International Criminal Court with new sanctions and an ultimatum
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The international criminal court (ICC) in The Hague. Photograph: Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP/Getty Images The United States was accused of launching “an assault” on the world’s legal order after imposing more sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) . Unveiling the Trump administration’s latest escalation against the court, which it has accused of politicization and unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, declared: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.” The ICC accused Donald Trump’s officials of attempting to “obstruct the course of justice” as Rubio, just hours after a former ICC judge was awarded the Nobel peace prize, announced in a video that the US would move to impose financial sanctions. Related: Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us. Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on X. “We don’t need that court and we don’t want it.” In a statement, the court warned that “history will judge this moment” and urged other members to ensure it can continue the function. “It is an ⁠attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what ⁠it was created to do. It is an assault ​on the rule ‌of law and ‌on the very foundations of the international legal order,” ‌the ICC said. The new set of sanctions will block any assets the ICC has in US jurisdictions and gives US companies or individuals six months to wind down business with the tribunal court. But the sanctions also allow the ICC to address the US government’s concerns, and certain transactions are exempt. The Trump administration has repeatedly condemned the ICC for issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. It also opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, although the case has been closed. The ICC was established in 2002 as an international tribunal to hold countries accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. Trump has long targeted the ICC. During his first term, he imposed sanctions on the court, which were later reversed under the Biden administration. But when Trump returned to office in 2025, he signed an executive order imposing sanctions on the ICC for the court’s investigations into Israelis and Americans. From there, the administration has continued to impose more sanctions. The administration added sanctions on judges and lawyers at the ICC. In August, it placed additional sanctions on the ICC president, Tomoko Akane. item.title: New Paxton recording exposes lingering GOP divisions in a tight Texas Senate race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks during a campaign event in Houston, on September 21. - Antranik Tavitian/Getty Images Ken Paxton has publicly said he would “love to have” John Cornyn’s support after their bruising Republican primary runoff in the Texas Senate race. But privately, Paxton has grown frustrated with the outgoing senator’s distance from his campaign. “He’s clearly not helping. He wants me to lose,” the Texas attorney general said at a fundraiser last month, according to an audio recording obtained by CNN from an attendee who opposes Paxton. While Paxton has minimized his criticism of Cornyn following their runoff, the private remarks demonstrate how their long-running tensions continue to roil the race, coming as national Republicans mount an all-out effort to help Paxton defeat Democratic state Rep. James Talarico . With polls showing a tight race, Republicans have poured well over $100 million into the general election in Texas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994 but is now critical to Republican hopes of holding a Senate majority. Paxton made the comments at a September 24 gathering in Washington after receiving a question about Rep. Jasmine Crockett, the Democratic congresswoman whom Talarico defeated in his primary, according to two sources familiar with the discussion. The recording obtained by CNN begins with Paxton apparently referencing Crockett, who has not campaigned for Talarico, saying he does not “know how much she really affects votes.” “I mean maybe a little bit around the margins, just like Cornyn, basically how much he affects me,” Paxton said. After saying Cornyn wants him to lose, Paxton pointed to a recent encounter that he said a friend had with the senator at a Dallas restaurant. Paxton said the friend bought Cornyn’s table dessert and sought to thank him for “supporting the ticket” — and for “supporting Ken Paxton” — and Cornyn reacted angrily. “Cornyn’s face went red. He backed off,” Paxton said. “He said, ‘Paxton’s gonna lose. We need to teach those Republicans a lesson. It’s going to be hard to learn, but they need to know that their decisions have consequences.’” “That’s what he’s trying to do,” Paxton said. “That’s John Cornyn.” CNN has not independently confirmed Paxton’s account, and a Cornyn representative, Rob Jesmer, told CNN that the conversation at the restaurant did not happen. “If Sen. Cornyn wanted Ken to lose, I can assure you he’d be more active in the campaign,” Jesmer, a longtime political strategist for Cornyn, said. “He has said he supports the Republican ticket. Given all Ken has said and done, I think that’s a pretty good place for Sen. Cornyn to be.” Asked for comment on the audio, Paxton’s campaign dismissed it as “a story that doesn’t exist” but noted that Paxton “has called, texted, and offered to have a conversation with Senator Cornyn.” “Like all Texans, General Paxton appreciates his decades of service to the Lone Star State,” Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement. “We hope he will join us in our fight to preserve the institution that is the United States Senate and help save our majority.” The two lobbyists who hosted the fundraising event, Chris Brinson and Susan Hirschmann, did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Talarico’s campaign. A spokesperson for Crockett said she has taken a different approach than Cornyn since losing her own primary. “Cornyn is the sitting senator and continues to attack his party’s nominee,” the spokesperson, Karrol Rimal, said in a statement. “Crockett endorsed Talarico on March 4th and has not stopped working to support Democrats across the nation since.” Continued problems for Paxton’s campaign Paxton’s problems with his own base, including former Cornyn supporters, have loomed over the final weeks of the race. A Paxton campaign memo dated Tuesday, reported by Punchbowl News , told supporters that the “biggest challenge we face is shoring up Republicans following a bruising primary.” A Fox News poll done late last month found that nearly a third of Republican likely voters had an unfavorable opinion of Paxton. While he was winning 90% of GOP voters, about a fifth of “non-MAGA” Republicans were breaking for Talarico. The clip obtained by CNN is at least the fifth recording that has leaked from the fundraising event last month and put Paxton’s campaign on the defensive in the final weeks of the race. Previous clips have featured Paxton saying the GOP’s midterm convention damaged him politically and that he feels like he has lost “control” over his campaign as outside groups have handled most of the spending. President Donald Trump, who backed Paxton in the primary, has said he is “worried” about the Texas race but largely declined to address the recordings when asked about them. He said Wednesday he was not second-guessing his endorsement. “I would have no regrets at all,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. The president visited San Antonio on Wednesday night for a rally with Paxton where he praised him as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.” Years of bad blood The bad blood between Cornyn and Paxton goes back years. Cornyn, who served as Texas attorney general from 1999 to 2002, has long made clear that he believes Paxton has disgraced the office and served as an example of what happens when Republicans do not police their own. Paxton has dished it back, painting Cornyn as a relic of a bygone era of Republican politics in Texas, especially after Cornyn ushered through a bipartisan gun safety law in 2022. Sen. John Cornyn, on Capitol Hill on August 4. - Win McNamee/Getty Images When Paxton faced a competitive primary for reelection in 2022, Cornyn did not make an endorsement but said Paxton’s long-running indictment on state securities fraud charges was an “embarrassment.” The case finally ended two years later with a deal where Paxton agreed to do community service and pay restitution . After Paxton was acquitted in a state Senate impeachment trial in 2023, which centered on allegations he abused his office to help a donor, he wasted little time teasing a potential run against Cornyn in 2026. “Everything’s on the table,” he told former Fox News host Tucker Carlson in a triumphant interview days after the trial. “Hard to run from prison, Ken,” Cornyn said in a February 2024 social media post after Paxton called for Texans to elect a new senator in 2026. Paxton, who denies all wrongdoing, launched his campaign in April 2025 with a promise to “send John Cornyn packing.” Cornyn and allied groups unleashed tens of millions of dollars of bitter, negative ads against Paxton, some of them highlighting allegations of infidelity. Cornyn finished narrowly ahead of Paxton in the primary but did not earn enough support to avoid a runoff against Paxton. “I refuse to allow a flawed, self-centered and shameless candidate like Ken Paxton to risk everything we’ve worked so hard to build over these many years,” Cornyn said on primary night, adding, “Judgment Day is coming for Ken Paxton.” But Trump ultimately had other plans. He endorsed Paxton a week before the runoff, dealing a crushing blow to Cornyn and his hopes of stopping a fellow Republican who, to him, embodied much of what is wrong with the modern GOP. ‘He was not my first choice’ Cornyn had long promised to support the “Republican ticket” regardless of the outcome of the primary. But since losing, he has avoided helping Paxton and even leaned into his frustrations with the nominee and his wing of the party at times. The senator criticized Paxton as a “poor campaigner” and “lazy” candidate in an August interview with the Texas Tribune . Cornyn and former President George W. Bush headlined a fundraiser in Dallas last month for six Senate GOP candidates in battleground races – but not Paxton. Cornyn’s refusal to endorse Paxton has annoyed some Texas GOP leaders, including Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a top Trump ally in the state. Patrick suggested in June, following the primary runoff, that Cornyn was part of “sore losers undermining our party.” Talarico, meanwhile, has sought to appeal to people who supported Cornyn in the GOP primary. He told CNN last month that he hopes to “live up to” Cornyn’s legacy and that he welcomes the incumbent’s supporters to “join this movement we’re building.” The Democrat’s campaign even hired a former staffer in Cornyn’s office over the summer. Cornyn defended the staffer’s move amid some intraparty backlash, saying on X that “those concerned might want to channel their energy into broadening R[epublican] outreach.” Some prominent supporters of Cornyn from the primary continue to show reluctance about voting for Paxton. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Ken Paxton during a campaign rally in San Antonio on October 7. - Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images “I’m supporting the party, but he was not my first choice, and I do think it’s going to have an impact down-ballot,” Rep. Michael McCaul of Texas told CNN last month. “And I do think there are Republicans … that may just not vote, and that’s the danger.” Paxton has made some headway with his intra-party opponents. In the weeks after the primary runoff, he was joined on the campaign trail by state Rep. Jeff Leach, who endorsed Cornyn in the primary and served as a leader in the 2023 impeachment case against Paxton. Yet some Texas Republicans continue to worry that GOP voters could simply skip the race. Ken Paxton’s estranged wife, Angela Paxton, addressed that possibility during a recent speech to a group of GOP women, urging them to set aside their reservations with any particular candidate for the good of the party. “When you can’t vote for, then vote against,” she said, “but vote.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/09/politics/ken-paxton-audio-john-cornyn

item.title: Social platforms prohibit violent content. Will an execution livestream count?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's revelation that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be streamed live has drawn fierce criticism and calls for him to reconsider his plan. But it has also put the spotlight on whether social media companies will allow government accounts to stream the death by firing squad on their platforms. Hegseth has not provided additional details about the Defense Department's plans to livestream the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009. Hasan is set to die by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, the defense secretary said. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. The defense chief did not say how the execution would be streamed, and whether the Pentagon would provide that content through its social media accounts or on its website. But his comments Thursday, made to far-right political activist Jack Posobiec, provide advance warning to social media companies that the content could be posted to their platforms. "If this were a private entity who said, 'we're going to be executing someone at this date,' I think platforms would just say, 'you can't use our platform,'" David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told CBS News. "The only reason this is even a little bit more difficult of a decision for the platforms is because this is the government doing it, and there is some interest in the public understanding and being able to witness barbaric acts of its government, and there will also likely be pressure from the government to carry it." Google, Meta, TikTok and X, which operate the nation's most popular social media platforms, all have policies governing violent or graphic content. Google, Meta and X did not respond to questions about whether they would allow the Defense Department to livestream Hasan's execution on their platforms or whether that content would violate their rules. A spokesperson for TikTok U.S. pointed to its policy on "shocking and graphic content," which states that the platform does not allow "anything extremely gory, disturbing, or violent, especially when it could cause psychological harm." "Some content that's less graphic or shared in the public interest may be allowed, but it may be viewable only for users 18 and older or ineligible" for its For You Feed, TikTok's policy states. That includes "graphic footage of events that would otherwise violate our rules but are in the public interest to view, such as wars and major disasters." Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, explicitly states in its "violent and graphic content" policy that it does not allow "live-streams of capital punishments." "We recognize that users may share content in order to shed light on or condemn acts such as human rights abuses or armed conflict," Meta's rules read. "Our policies consider when content shared in this context and allow room for discussion and awareness raising accordingly." YouTube, operated by Google, has guidelines covering violent or graphic content, as well as harmful or dangerous content. YouTube's harmful or dangerous content policy bars "acts performed by adults that have a risk of serious harm or death," or "content that encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death." The violent or graphic content policy states that YouTube does not allow "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers." The company tells users not to post content that includes "footage or imagery showing bodily fluids, such as blood or vomit, with the intent to shock or disgust viewers" or "footage of corpses with massive injuries, such as severed limbs." YouTube also has rules specifically governing content that involves guns and says it prohibits "live streams that show someone holding, handling, or transporting a firearm." X, which is owned by billionaire Elon Musk, prohibits "violent media that we consider high in severity and likelihood of harm." Its policy covers "gratuitous gore" and "moment of death." Violent content is barred "within areas that are highly visible" on the platform, including live video. The social media platform considers "gratuitous gore" to be "media of humans or animals that depicts excessively graphic or gruesome content related to death, violence or severe physical harm," including "dismembered or mutilated humans." X says it may request the removal of "images or videos that were taken at the point of, immediately before, or after an identifiable individual's death, if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative." Some social media companies like Facebook and YouTube tightened their policies on harmful content in the wake of the 2019 attack at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, when a gunman livestreamed the massacre. Years earlier, they scrambled to take down graphic videos of brutal executions by Islamic State militants. But social media companies have also been encouraged to ensure content showing human rights abuses or war crimes is preserved. Greene said it would be up to the platforms to decide whether to allow content like an execution by firing squad to be streamed, even if it may violate their policies. And because the Defense Department has telegraphed its plans to show the killing, Greene said he expects people inside the companies to decide whether to allow the footage on their platforms, rather than waiting for it to be flagged by automated systems. Executions outside of the military justice system are typically observed by members of the media, who serve as representatives of the public and provide a look into what capital punishment entails, Greene said. But he stressed that when deciding whether to allow Hasan's execution to be streamed live, social media companies should consider the U.S. government's motives. "This seems to be the government wanting to broadcast the execution for propaganda purposes and wanting to glorify its ability to execute people," he said. If Hegseth follows through with his plan to livestream Hasan's execution, it would place the United States in a small group of nations that are carrying out public executions. There were at least 17 known public executions in 2025: six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran, according to Amnesty International . In the U.S., it appears the last public execution took place in 1936. Then, a crowd of an estimated 20,000 gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. item.title: FBI arrests another ShinyHunters suspect after its own website was hacked
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The FBI's top official on Oct. 9 announced that the agency had arrested another suspected member of ShinyHunters , the digital hacking group accused of stealing personnel data from the FBI's jobs site in September. "This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly," FBI Director Kash Patel posted on X . Patel, who did not release the identity of the person arrested, said the breach took place on a platform managed by a third-party vendor. The New York Times is reporting that the suspect is a Canadian citizen and was arrested in Pennsylvania. Officials have not said how the group − which the FBI is calling "a global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world" − gained access to FBIjobs.gov . But Reuters previously reported that an internal memo distributed across the FBI said officials were operating under the assumption that all current and former employees had been exposed. USA TODAY has reached out to the FBI for more information. The arrest comes on the heels of Patel, on Sept. 29, announcing that Dutch National Police had arrested one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters. In a statement posted on X one day earlier, Dutch police announced that they had arrested a 24-year-old man suspected of playing a role with ShinyHunters. Police also did not name that man, but Reuters reported that Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security said it was Pepijn van der Stap, the company's offensive security lead. Korper said Dutch investigators visited his office Sept. 15 – the same day van der Stap was arrested in a police raid that involved flash bang grenades . FBI Assistant Director Brett Leatherman said the cybercriminals have allegedly breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments. The group, Leatherman said, often targets "third-party vendors in cloud-based platforms, stealing sensitive data and extorting victims with threats to publish it." The case remained under investigation on Oct. 9, Patel said. Contributing: Reuters Natalie Neysa Alund is a senior reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at nalund@usatoday.com and follow her on X @nataliealund . item.title: 'It was quid pro quo': Businessman says Guilfoyle offered political access for $100,000
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Businessman Eric Deters said he has "no doubt it was pay to play," claiming Kimberly Guilfoyle, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of Guilfoyle's Senate confirmation hearing. In an interview with CBS News, Deters said Guilfoyle should "lose her ambassadorship" over her alleged behavior, after texts between the two of them from last July were published in the Wall Street Journal . "It was quid pro quo," Deters told CBS News White House correspondent Weijia Jiang Thursday. Deters said he never gave her the money. "Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it." Deters said he made up an "excuse" that his wife wouldn't go along with it. White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said. The Wall Street Journal first reported this week that Guilfoyle allegedly reached out to Deters days before her congressional hearing to become a U.S. ambassador, saying she needed $100,000 to pay off her American Express credit debt in a way that wouldn't be publicly visible. "It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that's all that will show," Guilfoyle wrote to Deters on July 3, according to screen shots of texts provided to CBS News. "I have been officially announced honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote, punctuating the message with a prayer-hands emoji. Her confirmation hearing took place on July 9. She sent him "American Express Instructions" in a PDF document. CBS News has reviewed the texts, which were provided by Deters as part of a 292-page file that included dozens of pages of grievances against Trump world figures, communications with Guilfoyle and others, photos of Deters with Guilfoyle, President Trump, Eric Trump and Trump Jr., and a lengthy excerpt of a book Deters has written. CBS News has reached out to spokespeople for the State Department and the White House, as well as Guilfoyle. Deters, a longtime Trump supporter, is a retired lawyer and businessman from Kentucky who was sanctioned by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2021 for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law. He has also run unsuccessfully for Kentucky governor and for Rep. Thomas Massie's U.S. House seat. For years, Deters has been trying to attract media attention and political support for a push to extradite orthopedic spine surgeon Dr. Abubakar Durrani . The government believes Durrani fled the country while he was awaiting trial for healthcare fraud charges. He was accused of billing Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance companies millions of dollars for unnecessary spinal surgeries that were potentially harmful to patients. Today, Deters said he feels slighted that he never received support for his push to have Durrani extradited to the U.S. from influential Trump world figures. "I sent Susie Wiles, Don Jr. and Kimberly Guilfoyle an email, and I told them, I said, 'You got until 5 o'clock on Monday to help me out with the Durrani victims,'" he said. "They didn't respond. And I told them, 'If you don't, I'm going to go to the media and try to get the media's help because you're not helping.' So I gave them one last shot, and they ignored me." In the text messages reviewed by CBS News, Deters, who said he also represents hundreds of Durrani's former patients, may have believed he could benefit from Durrani's extradition to the U.S. He wrote to Trump Jr. and Guilfoyle's podcast producer, Drew Lynch, and suggested, "If anyone in Don Jr or your world has an interest in listening to a pitch on how lots of money could be made for a little money in this Durrani matter let me know." Deters, who no longer practices law, once stood to gain financially if he were able to successfully sue Durrani. Just before he took office in 2025 and soon after Guilfoyle and Trump Jr. broke off their engagement, Mr. Trump announced he planned to nominate Guilfoyle to be U.S. ambassador to Greece. But Deters said her influence has waned since her relationship with Trump Jr. ended. "There was no question that she would do anything for me," Deters said. "The problem was, she was on the outs of the Trump world." Deters claimed Guilfoyle knew there was something wrong about asking for the payment. "She knew there was something wrong about it because she kept getting mad at me," Deters said. "I mean, I'm naive, I'm putting stuff in writing, sending it to her. She's getting mad. She wants me to use Signal. I didn't know what Signal was." In late June 2025, she texted, "Eric, I really wish you would stop papering these things. It's really dangerous and not helpful to you and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal." Deters had just sent her a memo to complain that she had not delivered on things that he had asked of her, including getting him booked on Tucker Carlson's podcast. "I generously offered you $1 million dollars when Durrani settles if you got me on Tucker," he wrote. He also complained that he had prepared a "concise summary" for then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, but "I have not received nothing concrete." Deters also sought a meeting with then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long about a tax issue, and he wanted Guilfoyle to send the lyrics to a song he had written to Kid Rock. Deters said in the memo, "I am not naive or a sucker. I need results. No results. No need for me to pay." He prodded her over text soon afterward: "As of this moment, I bet there have been no emails AND phone calls by you to Wells [Tucker Carlson's producer], Bondi, Long." Guilfoyle said his accusation was "completely false" and sent as proof the PDF of a letter in which she congratulated Long on his confirmation and asked him to give his attention to Deters' tax issue. Deters claimed he has paid Guilfoyle and members of the Trump family in the past. "I paid her a total of $300,000," he said. "Don, Jr. $200,000 for two appearances. Eric Trump for $100,000, $125,000 for President Trump's PAC, $100,000 to go to Kentucky Derby with Trump. So, I paid a lot of money to Trump World," he said, adding that he never owed money to Guilfoyle or anyone else around Mr. Trump. According to the documents he shared with CBS News, he says he paid Guilfoyle a total of $300,000 for appearance fees. And he said his promise of further payments to Guilfoyle and Lynch was to be for their services as consultants. The Trump administration's response so far In Greece, where Guilfoyle greeted his plane earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio chastised reporters for asking about the matter. "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel," he said. "It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things." Rubio also declined to comment because the story had only "literally posted a few hours ago," telling reporters that "we don't conduct these things in a press conference, on a tarmac, in a foreign country." As Rubio departed Greece, Guilfoyle was present, but off to the side . CBS News on Thursday asked Vice President JD Vance about the propriety of a government official asking someone to pay off their debt. CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs asked: "Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange to access to other government officials?" "With that hypothetical, obviously I don't love that, but I, you know, I don't know exactly who you're talking about. I don't know the full details," Vance responded. Deters insisted his relationship with Guilfoyle was purely political. "Kimberly Guilfoyle and I have absolutely zero personal relationship, nada," he told CBS News. But Deters is now determined to share his story. He said he wants to draw attention to Dr. Durrani's victims. And he wants Guilfoyle out of her post as U.S. ambassador. "I'm a tough hombre," Deters said. "I'm going to get to take Kimberly Guilfoyle's deposition." item.title: Democrats unite around Hegseth impeachment push
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The News Congressional Democrats aren’t eager to impeach Donald Trump. Pete Hegseth is a different story. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his leadership circle remain reluctant to lean too far into talking about impeaching the president if they regain power next month, a move that would revive the bruising battles of Trump’s first term. But as the Iran war squeezes Republicans ahead of the midterms, Democrats are aligning to call for the defense secretary’s ouster or resignation. With impeachment still a dirty word among many House Democrats, targeting Cabinet secretaries could be a pressure release valve for lawmakers itching for action against the Trump administration. “I 100% believe Pete Hegseth needs to be impeached and removed from office, because not only is he the worst secretary of defense in American history, he is a dangerous war criminal,” said Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., who said it should be one of the caucus’ “top three priorities” next year. Hegseth was reviled by the left even before the Iran war began, and since then he’s faced criticism from Republicans for his handling of the war. An impeachment vote could even be bipartisan: When the House returns after the midterms, it’ll be forced to take up a Hegseth ouster resolution filed by iconoclastic Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Prioritizing Hegseth impeachment would solve a big problem for Democrats: If they win the House, their leaders will face intense pressure from the base to show a new level of fight against Trump. Yet they’re leery of the internal divisions or appearance of overreach that a third Trump impeachment might create, and still smarting from his return to office after two impeachment votes. In public, top Democrats are accordingly circumspect on targeting Hegseth. Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired and that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything out” in their investigations. Democrats have filed impeachment articles against other Trump Cabinet officials, like Education Secretary Linda McMahon and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has also filed impeachment articles against Hegseth. Yet interviews with a half dozen Democrats pointed to Hegseth as the safest place to land. It’s not just safe-seat Democrats willing to take the plunge: Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represents a Trump-won district, said she was open to the possibility. “If I were Pete Hegseth, I’d be worried. It’s certainly something that needs serious consideration, and I hear Democrats, yes, but I also hear some Republicans saying it as well. I think there’s a lot he needs to answer for,” she said. Of course, it may not be even up to Democratic leaders in the end. Impeachment politics next year could be driven by an incoming crop of progressive lawmakers who could form a sizable bloc in the caucus. Any member can force a vote on an impeachment resolution, which outgoing Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, repeatedly triggered during Trump’s first term and his current one. “Pete Hegseth should be impeached. Congress never voted for a war with Iran, and he’s been running one since February anyway. It’s cost innocent lives and more than $40 billion of our money,” said Melat Kiros, a Colorado progressive who is heavily favored to win election to the House in November. Massie’s Hegseth resolution, among other allegations, lays out charges of violating Congress’ war powers and carrying out extrajudicial killings. “They all should be impeached — President Trump and his cabinet that’s enabled him to do everything that he has right now,” said Adam Hamawy, a fellow Justice Democrats-aligned progressive from New Jersey. “Now, whether we’re going to be able to do that is another thing, but it’s not something that, you know, we should just ignore because it’s not possible.” The Pentagon defended Hegseth’s record in a statement. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,” said Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson, adding that the Pentagon “is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before.” Know More It’s unclear if Hegseth will leave the administration post-midterms. While Trump is known to be unpredictable, he likes Hegseth a lot, and those familiar with the situation are skeptical of any looming changes at the top of the department. Still, other Democrats say they need to balance impeachment with acting on cost-of-living issues like healthcare that they believe will tip the midterms in their favor. “There’s going to have to be a balance of addressing needs and meeting our constituents where they’re at, and also part of restoring the faith of the American people in our own government and restoring the integrity of our democratic institutions — it requires holding bad actors to justice,” said Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J. The Massie resolution will be a good test for Democratic support for going after Hegseth. Some Democrats are loath to support a measure drafted by a Republican and before any kind of investigative process has been completed. But some leaders like Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Committee Democrat, have signaled they could back the Massie measure. The House has only ever impeached two Cabinet secretaries, with the most recent being the GOP-led impeachment of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. The then-Democratic Senate voted to toss the articles of impeachment. If Democrats take both the House and Senate next year, Hegseth could get a debilitating trial in the upper chamber. Nicholas’s view Taking on Hegseth is basically a free shot for Democrats. It allows them to demonstrate to the base that they could take action against the Trump administration without the risk of backlash that impeaching the president himself could bring. But they’ll only be able to keep a lid on the prospect of impeaching Trump for so long. With many in the party pushing for investigations of potential malfeasance by the administration, party leaders will face tough choices about consequences if those probes do turn up wrongdoing. And unlike 2018, when purple-district Democrats ran away from impeaching Trump, some are already embracing it. San Diego City Councilmember Marni von Wilpert, who’s running in a newly redrawn purple district, called recent comments by Trump about Iran’s ability to “take out” San Diego and Los Angeles an “impeachable offense.” Notable Democrats on the House Armed Services Committee are weighing the creation of an oversight subpanel to probe Hegseth’s department, Politico reported.
